result:
I found the cause and fixed it. All 72 tests in `tst_qcoreapplication` pass, including the two new ones, and `tst_qthread` and `tst_qobject` pass too. With the library change reverted, the new test hangs, so it does catch the bug.

## Root cause
When the application object is destroyed, `QCoreApplicationPrivate::cleanupThreadData()` deletes the events still waiting in the queue. It did this while holding the queue's lock, and that lock can't be taken twice by the same thread. If an event's destructor calls `postEvent()` or `deleteLater()` (which posts an event), it tries to take the same lock on the same thread and waits forever. That matches what you saw with the Windows Media Foundation backend.

A second copy of this cleanup, `QThreadData::clearEvents()`, deleted events without taking the lock at all. It had the opposite problem: other threads could change the queue while it was being emptied.

## Fix
- **`src/corelib/thread/qthread.cpp`**: `QThreadData::clearEvents()` is now the only implementation, following the approach in `CLAUDE.md`:
  - It takes all pending events out of the queue while holding the lock, resets the queue's counters and positions (`recursion`, `startOffset`, `insertionOffset`), and marks every event in the batch as no longer posted.
  - It then releases the lock and deletes the events. Nothing is deleted until the whole batch has been marked, because one destructor may destroy another receiver in the same batch.
  - Destructors can post new events, so it repeats until the queue is empty, up to 16 rounds. If events are still coming after that, it prints a warning and leaks what's left instead of looping forever. The limit of 16 is my choice; change it if you prefer another value.
- **`src/corelib/kernel/qcoreapplication.cpp`**: `cleanupThreadData()` now just calls `clearEvents()`.

## Tests
I added two tests to `tests/auto/corelib/kernel/qcoreapplication/`:
- **`postEventFromEventDestructorAtExit`**: an event still pending when the app is destroyed calls both `postEvent()` and `deleteLater()` from its destructor. It checks that nothing hangs and that the receiver ends with no pending events.
- **`endlesslyRepostingEventAtExit`**: an event's destructor always posts another such event. It checks that destruction stops, the leak warning is printed, and the counts end at zero.

When I ran the full suite inside a loop, five tests failed with "No program defined". Those tests start a helper program and only find it when run from the test's build directory. Run from there, all 72 pass.

Your message ended with some lines that looked pasted by mistake ("765378 K3b 1" and so on). I ignored them; tell me if they meant something.

Nothing is committed yet.
